Mujahid said: He meant only the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). al-Dahhak said: The intended meaning is the dawn of Dhu al-Hijjah. Muqatil said: The intended meaning is the dawn of the Night of Muzdalifah (laylat jam'). Ibn 'Abbas also said: The intended meaning is the dawn of the first day of Muharram, because it is the dawn of the year. It was also said: The intended meaning is the dawn of springs (fajr al-'uyun) from rocks and other things. 'Ikrimah said: The intended meaning is the dawn of Friday.

People differed regarding "the ten nights." Some narrators said: They are the first ten nights of Ramadan. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: They are the last ten nights of Ramadan. Yaman and a group of interpreters (al-muta'awwilun) said: They are the first ten days of Muharram, and in it is the Day of 'Ashura'. Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and 'Atiyya al-'Awfi said: They are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Mujahid also said: They are the ten nights of Moses, peace be upon him, which God the Exalted completed for him.

Others said: The even is the created being and the odd is God, glory be to Him, since He, the Exalted, is the One in an absolute sense, while others are not so. Some interpreters said: The even is Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, and the odd is God, glory and exaltation be to Him. Ibn Sirin, Masruq and Abu Salih said: The even and the odd are common to all creation: faith and disbelief, humans and jinn, and whatever follows this pattern; they are opposites or nearly opposites, and God made them an odd, single unity. Some exegetes said: The even is Eve and the odd is Adam, peace be upon them both. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: The odd is the Maghrib prayer and the even is the Subh prayer. Some scholars said: The even is the supererogatory night prayer offered in pairs (mathna mathna), and the odd is the well-known last rak'ah.

The majority of reciters and people recited "wa-l-witr" (وَالوَتَرِ) with a fatha on the waw, which is the dialect of Quraysh and the people of the Hijaz. *A glory, ancient, that its first built, who reached 'Ad, and before it, Iram.*

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak recited "bi-'Adi arramma" (بِعادِ إرَمَّ) with a shadda on the mim, as a past verb meaning: it decayed and became crumbled bones (rameem). It is said: "arima al-'azm" and "rumma" and "arammahu Allah," with "ramma" transitive by the hamza. Ibn 'Abbas also recited "armi dhata" (أرْمِ ذاتَ) with a fatha on the ta', in the sense that God brought decay upon it, meaning: your Lord wore it away and made it crumbled. The majority recited "lam yukhlaq" (لَمْ يُخْلَقْ) with a damma on the ya' and fatha on the lam, "mithluha" (مِثلُها) in the nominative. It was said: they are his soldiers by whom his rule was established. It was said the intended meaning is the tent-pegs of his armies, which were mentioned because of their number and because they indicate his military campaigns and his wandering through the lands. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and from it is the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

*...... in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes are firm.*

Qatadah said: He had stakes on which men would play before him while he overlooked them. Mujahid said: He would stake people with iron stakes, killing them by this, driving them into their bodies until they penetrated the ground. It was said: This was done to his wife Asiya; it was said: He did this to the hairdresser of his daughter, because she had believed in Moses, peace be upon him.

"Al-tughyan" (transgression) is exceeding the limits. "Al-sabb" (pouring) is used for the whip, because it requires swiftness in descent, and from it is the poet's saying about those accused of slander (in the affair of al-ifk):

*Then there poured upon them stinging scourges, as if they were showers, not from cloud nor from rain.*

And from it is the later poet's saying describing horses:

*We poured upon them, unjustly, our whips, so that there flew with them hands swift and feet.*

The whip was specifically chosen to be borrowed for punishment because it requires repetition and reiteration that the sword and other things do not require. Some lexicographers said: "al-sawt" here is a verbal noun from "saata yasuutu," so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: a mixture of punishment.

"Al-mirsad" and "al-marsad" are the place of watching (ristad), as the lexicographers said; that is, He is at the tongue of every speaker, and a watcher over every doer. On this interpretation of "al-mirsad," there is the answer of 'Amir ibn Qays to 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, when he said to him: "Where is your Lord, O Bedouin?" He said: "In the watch-place (bi-l-mirsad)." It is possible that "al-mirsad" in the verse is an active participle, as if He, the Exalted, said: "Indeed He is the watcher (labi-l-rasid)," and so He expressed it with the intensive form. It has been related in some hadith: "Indeed, over the bridge of Hell (jisr Jahannam) are three bridges (qanatir): on one is trust (al-amanah), on another is blood (al-dam), and on the last is the Lord, the Exalted. This is His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 89, verse 15–22:

The Exalted said:

﴿So as for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me."﴾ ﴿But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me."﴾ ﴿No! Rather, you do not honour the orphan,﴾ ﴿and do not urge one another to feed the poor,﴾ ﴿and you devour the inheritance, devouring greedily,﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with abundant love.﴾ ﴿No! When the earth is pounded to dust, pounded and crushed,﴾ ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.﴾

God, exalted is He, mentions in this verse what the Quraysh used to say and what they took as evidence of God's honouring or humiliating His servant. That is because they used to see that whoever has wealth, property and children from Him is honoured, and the opposite of that is humiliated. Since this section was predominantly applied to many of the disbelievers, the rebuke in this verse came in the generic form (ism al-jins), since some believers may fall into something of this outlook. Among that is the hadith of the Bedouins who used to come to Madina to the Prophet ﷺ: whoever gained good said, "This is a good religion," and whoever was afflicted with harm said, "This is an evil religion."

"Ibtalahu" means: tested him. "Na''amahu" means: made him one who possesses blessing (ni'ma). Ibn Kathir read "akramani" with a ya' both in pause and in continuation; ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i omitted it in both cases; Nafi' read it with a ya' in continuation and omitted it in pause, and likewise "ahanani"; Abu 'Amr allowed both options. The majority of readers read "faqadara" with a light dal, in a narrow sense (bi-ma'na ḍayyiq). Al-Hasan, with a variant report, Abu Ja'far, 'Isa and Khalid read "faqaddara" with a heavy dal, meaning: made it according to a measure (ʿalā qadr). It was said: both have the same meaning in the sense of restriction, because "qaddara" is intensive (mubalagha) not transitive; and the man's saying "ahanani" implies this, because "qadara" when transitive means only: He gave him what suffices him, and there is no humiliation along with that.

Then the Exalted said: "Kalla," as a rejection of their saying and belief, meaning: God's honouring and humiliating are not like that; rather that is a test. Whoever is tested with wealth should be thankful and obedient, and whoever is tested with poverty should be thankful and patient. As for God's honouring, it is by piety, and His humiliating is by disobedience. Then He informed them of their deeds, that they do not honour the orphan, who is—among the sons of Adam—one who has lost his father and was not yet of age, and among the animals one who has lost its mother. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 89, verses 23–30:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And on that Day Hell will be brought forward; on that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life."﴾ ﴿So on that Day none will punish as He punishes,﴾ ﴿and none will bind as He binds.﴾ ﴿"O reassured soul,﴾ ﴿return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him].﴾ ﴿So enter among My servants,﴾ ﴿and enter My Paradise."﴾

It has been narrated concerning His saying, ﴿And on that Day Hell will be brought forward﴾, that it will be driven to the Gathering (al-Hashr) with seventy thousand bridles, each bridle held by seventy thousand angels, and then a neck will emerge from it and seize the tyrants among the disbelievers... in a long hadith with varying wordings. And "Jahannam" here means the Fire in its entirety. It is also narrated that when the verse "And on that Day Hell will be brought forward" was revealed, the colour of the Prophet ﷺ changed.

As for His saying, ﴿on that Day man will remember﴾, its meaning is: he will remember his disobedience and his transgression, and he will look at the good deeds that he missed. Then He said, ﴿but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾, i.e., how will remembrance benefit him? Then He mentioned of him that he says, ﴿"Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life"﴾. The meaning of His saying "for my life" has been disputed. The majority of interpreters said: its meaning is "for my enduring life", meaning the Hereafter. Some of the interpreters said: the meaning is "for my life in my grave at my resurrection, which I used to deny and believed I would never return to life." And some said: "for my life" here is figurative, meaning: "Oh, I wish I had sent forth righteous deeds so that I might enjoy them today and live a good life", just as a person says, "Give me life in this matter." Some of the interpreters said: the meaning is "for a time" or "for the duration of my past life in this world," and this is like when you say, "I came for the rising of the sun and for such-and-such a date," and the like.

The majority of reciters, as well as ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, recited "yuʿadhdhibu" and "yūthiqu" with a kasra on the dhāl and the thāʾ. According to this reading, the pronoun in "ʿadhābahu" and "withāqahu" refers to God, Exalted is He, and the verbal noun is annexed to the agent. This has two meanings: first, that God, Exalted is He, does not entrust the punishment of the disbelievers that day to anyone; second, that His punishment is of such severity that no one has ever been punished with its like in this world. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the disbeliever, and the verbal noun is annexed to the object.

Al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Sīrīn, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and Sawwād al-Qāḍī recited "yuʿadhhabu" and "yūthaqu" with a fatḥa on the dhāl and the thāʾ, and I have narrated this widely from the Prophet ﷺ. Then the two pronouns, according to this reading, refer to the disbeliever who stands in the position of his entire kind, and the verbal noun is annexed to the object, and "ʿadhāb" is placed in the position of "taʿdhīb", as in the line of poetry:

"And after your giving, the hundred camels grazing (?)"

It is also possible that the two pronouns in this reading refer to God, Exalted is He, as if He, glorified is He, said: no one ever punishes in this world with the punishment of God for the disbelievers. Then the verbal noun is annexed to the agent, but this interpretation is strained. Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad recited "withāqahu" with a kasra on the wāw.

When the mention of these punished ones was finished, God, Exalted is He, followed it with mention of the souls of the believers and their condition, saying, ﴿O reassured soul﴾, and so on. The meaning of "al-muṭma'inna" is: the one who is certain to the utmost degree of certainty. Do you not see that Abraham, peace be upon him, said, "but that my heart may be at rest"? So it is a rank above faith, and it is that the soul, in its certainty, has no remaining goal that moves it to attain it.

People differed about when this call occurs. Ibn Zayd and others said: it is at the moment the soul of the believer leaves his body in this world. It has been narrated that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about this, and he said to him: "The angel will say it to you, O Abū Bakr, at your death." The meaning of ﴿return to your Lord﴾ according to this interpretation is: return with death. And His saying, ﴿among My servants﴾, means: among the number of My righteous servants, and this is the reading of the majority with the plural "ʿibādī". It has been said: the call is at the raising of bodies from the graves, so His saying, ﴿return to your Lord﴾ means: by resurrection from your death, return to God, Exalted is He.
